beliefs.practice: Use a single, long-lived MongoClient instance (singleton) per Node.js process; do not create a new client per request or per change-stream event.

Never store DOCUMENTDB connection strings or credentials in code or repo; read them from environment variables (e.g., DOCUMENTDB_URI) and prefer a secrets store (Azure Key Vault) in deployments; include only a .env.example with placeholders.
Require TLS/SSL for connections and enable server certificate validation in the MongoDB driver options (do not disable ssl/TLS verification in production).
Configure sensible connection options on the MongoClient (maxPoolSize/minPoolSize, connectTimeoutMS, socketTimeoutMS, keepAlive) tuned for the workload rather than using driver defaults.

Enable and rely on driver-level retryableReads/retryableWrites where available, and implement application-level exponential backoff for idempotent retries; avoid silent infinite retries for non-idempotent actions like sending messages.

When using change streams, persist the latest resume token (or operationTime) to durable storage and on restart resume the stream from that token (resumeAfter/startAtOperationTime) to avoid missing or duplicating events.

Handle resumable and non-resumable change stream errors explicitly (catch resumable errors and attempt resume, persist resume tokens frequently, and in case of non-resumable errors fall back to a safe recovery plan such as re-reading a time-window of events).

Choose a partition/shard key at collection creation with high cardinality and even distribution (e.g., customer_id) and declare it at creation time—do not rely on a collection being unpartitioned if you expect scale.

Create indexes for every field used in query predicates and sort keys (e.g., customer_id, event_type, event_timestamp, outreach_status) and verify index usage with explain(); do index creation idempotently during app bootstrap.

Create compound indexes that match common query patterns and field order (for example { customer_id:1, event_timestamp:-1 } for recent customer events) instead of relying on multiple single-field indexes.
For queries that return large documents or many fields, use projection to return only the fields needed (e.g., exclude large embedding arrays unless required) to reduce network and RU/IO usage.

Persist embeddings in a dedicated field and create a vector index with explicit parameters (dimension, metric, and index tuning such as HNSW M/efConstruction or DiskANN/IVF params); set search-time ef/search parameters for accuracy/latency tradeoffs consistently between indexing and querying.
Normalize embedding vectors consistently (e.g., L2-normalize for cosine similarity) at write time and ensure the same normalization is applied to query vectors.
If outreach logs are temporary or subject to a retention policy, use a TTL index on a timestamp field to automatically expire old logs instead of manual deletes.

Make seeding and index-creation scripts idempotent: check for collection existence and use createIndexes (which is idempotent) or catch duplicate-key errors so running the script multiple times is safe.
Use transactions only when you need atomic multi-document operations; keep transactions small and short-lived and be prepared to retry transient transaction errors with backoff.

Instrument and monitor database metrics (connection pool usage, active connections, ops/sec, latency, RU/sec or equivalent, index miss ratio) and capture slow query traces; use explain() to validate important queries in CI or during bootstrap.

Implement idempotency for external side effects (e.g., sending outreach): include an idempotency key (event id, outreach_id) in outreach_logs and check it before sending to avoid duplicate messages if an event is replayed.

Persist change-stream consumer progress (resume tokens, last processed event id/time) in a small, durable collection with a majority writeConcern so a crash or restart can resume exactly where it left off.

Avoid unbounded aggregation or map-reduce on hot collections in the change-stream consumer; batch process events, apply backpressure, and limit concurrency to avoid overwhelming the DB or exceeding provisioned throughput.
Do not log full PII or credentials; redact sensitive customer attributes in logs and in any persisted debug traces or stack dumps that could be stored in outreach_logs or monitoring exports.
